newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Rangebound trade, eye on dollar.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Rangebound trade, eye on dollar.

text.p: A lack of top-tier economic data on Friday is expected to subdue trading activity, leaving U.S. Treasury prices in a narrow range, analysts said.
After rallying during the past week on mostly bond-friendly economic news, Treasuries might have reached their peaks for now, market participants said.
They said Friday's scheduled data probably would not be able to carry Treasuries beyond their current levels.
The 30-year Treasury bond was priced at 99-9/32, up 3/32 and yielding 6.68 percent at 1500 EDT/1900 GMT on Thursday.
"For the market to stage another leg up, we would have to close through some of these (resistance) areas fairly convincingly," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co.
"It doesn't look like we are going to get the data to support that notion," he conceded.

The Treasury Department is slated to release its monthly budget for May at 1400 EDT/1800 GMT. On average, economists in a Reuters poll forecast a $49.97 billion budget deficit in May versus a $93.94 billion surplus in April.
Economists said that only a large deviation from Wall Street's consensus forecast could spur any excitement.
"The Treasury statement would have to be very far off consensus in either direction to really move the market," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.
What the Treasury market desires is confirmation that the economic slowdown -- suggested by a softening in May retail sales and consumer prices -- might continue beyond the second quarter, he said.

With little data on the menu, Low said the market might get some reaction after the Philadelphia Federal Reserve Bank releases its semiannual Livingston survey, a national survey of economists' projections on 18 different variables. The survey is scheduled for release at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT.

William Sullivan, senior vice president and director of fixed-income research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc, said the dollar performance vis a vis the market's perceptions of an ongoing Group of Seven summit in Denver might occupy center stage in the absence of any salient economic data.

"Don't expect a communique, but what we're suggesting is that maybe the exchange markets are affected by the perceptions created by that important meeting in terms of Japanese trade, the need to control budget deficits and the euro," he said.
Any significant dollar reaction could wash over on to Treasuries, Sullivan said, adding that "right now it seems to be a low probability scenario."
"Even looking for the exchange markets to influence Treasuries is pushing the envelope as well," he added.
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open near 5-7/16 percent on Friday.
